claim: Claude Opus 5.5 defaults to `medium` effort, down from `high` on Opus 5.
why: The source tells integrators to set effort explicitly and re-run their sweep instead of carrying over the Claude Opus 5 setting.
check: On routes migrating from Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, check whether effort was set explicitly and tested on the workload.
quote: Start at `medium`, the default on Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Opus 5 defaults to `high`), set it explicitly, and test several levels against your own evals

claim: In Anthropic’s tests, Opus 5.5 at `medium` matched or beat Opus 5 at `high` on coding and knowledge work, and `low` came close at much lower cost on several coding evaluations.
why: The source reports this from Anthropic testing and warns against mapping levels one-to-one.
check: When migrating to Opus 5.5, check whether the setup retested effort levels on its own evaluations before carrying over an Opus 5 setting.
quote: Effort level names don’t correspond to the same amount of thinking across models: in Anthropic’s testing, Claude Opus 5.5 at `medium` matches or exceeds Claude Opus 5 at `high` on coding and knowledge-work evaluations, and on several coding evaluations `low` comes close to it at much lower cost.

claim: At the same effort level, Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Opus 5, especially at `xhigh` and `max`.
why: Carrying over the same setting can mean longer turns and more output tokens, and a cap sized for thinking off can cut replies short.
check: Flag Opus 5.5 setups that run `xhigh` or `max` by default without a measured quality gain.
quote: At a given level, Claude Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Claude Opus 5, especially at `xhigh` and `max`.

claim: To make Opus 5.5 think less, lower the effort level before adding prompt instructions to think less.
why: Lowering effort reduces thinking, cost and latency more reliably than prompt wording does.
check: Look in Opus 5.5 instruction files for lines like 'don't overthink' or 'think briefly' used in place of a lower effort setting.
quote: Lowering effort reduces thinking, and with it cost and latency, more reliably than prompt instructions do.

claim: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 require adaptive thinking and return 400 for requests that disable thinking or set a manual thinking budget.
why: Opus 5 accepted `disabled` at effort `high` or below; Opus 5.5 removed that option.
check: Check outgoing requests to Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.1 for `thinking.type: disabled` or manual `thinking.type: enabled` with `budget_tokens`.
quote: On Claude Opus 5.5, thinking is always on: a request that sets `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}`, or one that sets a manual budget with `thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}`, returns a 400 `invalid_request_error`.

claim: When migrating an Opus 5 route that disabled thinking, start Opus 5.5 at `low` effort, measure latency and quality, and try `medium` if quality drops.
why: At `low`, Opus 5.5 keeps thinking short, while how often it skips thinking depends on the prompt.
check: For migrated thinking-off routes, check latency and quality at `low`, and retest quality if a prompt such as ‘Answer directly without deliberating’ is added to reduce time to first token.
quote: At `low` the model keeps its thinking short. How often it skips thinking altogether depends on your prompts, so measure latency and quality on your own traffic and move to `medium` if quality drops.

claim: On Opus 5.5, replace instructions that ask it to reproduce its internal reasoning in the reply with reading summarized `thinking` blocks, since such prompts can trigger `reasoning_extraction` refusals.
why: The guide distinguishes requests for internal reasoning from short explanations or summaries of actions, which it says users can still ask for.
check: Flag prompts that ask Opus 5.5 to reproduce its internal deliberation in the reply.
quote: A prompt that pushes the model to reproduce its reasoning in the response text might be declined with the `reasoning_extraction`

claim: On Opus 5.5, remove rules that prohibit thinking and retest the combined tool-use and internal-tag instruction used with thinking disabled on Opus 5.
why: Those mitigations addressed artifacts that appeared on Opus 5 only when thinking was disabled.
check: Flag no-thinking rules and check whether the old combined instruction about pre-tool text, what to do when no tool fits, and internal tags still helps.
quote: With thinking always on, check whether you still need the instruction, and remove the no-thinking rule either way.

claim: On long multipart tasks, Opus 5.5 can end a turn with a progress update and `stop_reason: end_turn`, so an unattended loop that equates this with task completion can stop early.
why: A text-only end of turn can be a progress report while task items remain open.
check: Check whether unattended Opus 5.5 loops evaluate completion against a checklist or another stated condition before stopping on a text-only turn.
quote: Treat a text-only end of turn as a report rather than as proof the task is done.

claim: For unattended Opus 5.5 runs, the guide suggests naming open checklist items in a follow-up when a turn ends without a blocker and capping automatic continuations at two or three per task.
why: The cap lets a genuinely stuck run end so it can be reviewed.
check: Check the continuation cap and whether follow-ups name open checklist items or explain which stated completion condition remains unmet.
quote: stop after two or three automatic continuations on the same task rather than repeating them indefinitely

claim: A standing system instruction that names which early stops to avoid and when to stop can reduce premature handoffs in fully unattended Opus 5.5 runs.
why: The guide’s example distinguishes a progress report from a blocker that actually needs the user.
check: When a fully unattended agent stops early, check whether the prompt covers announcing next steps without acting, offering to continue, pausing for nonblocking decisions, or stopping just to report.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 is responsive to instructions that name the specific kinds of early stop you want it to avoid, such as ending the turn with a summary that announces the next step instead of taking it. It also helps to name the stops you do want, for example when no work can advance without the user’s input.

claim: Use the Opus 5.5 unattended-run instruction from the first request and keep it out of human-in-the-loop applications.
why: Adding it partway through invalidates earlier thinking blocks, and using it can result in more tool calls and output tokens.
check: If a fully unattended harness uses the instruction, check that it starts in the first request and that the application keeps a confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.
quote: leave the addition out of human-in-the-loop applications, where someone is there to answer.

claim: Opus 5.5 progress notes between tool calls can arrive in `thinking` blocks whose text is empty at the default display, leaving a text-only client quiet during long turns.
why: The migration guide says notes longer than a sentence or two use progress-update blocks, while the prompting guide describes the change without that qualifier.
check: For a UI intended to show these notes, check for `thinking.display: updates` with the beta header or `summarized`, and render non-empty progress text.
quote: On Claude Opus 5.5 these notes come back as [progress-update `thinking` blocks](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking#progress-updates) rather than `text` blocks, and their text is empty at the default `thinking.display`.

claim: With `display: updates`, an Opus 5.5 harness can append a turn-scoped reminder after several silent tool steps and stop sending reminders after two or three if the turn stays quiet.
why: In Anthropic’s agentic coding tests, this roughly halved the share of tasks with a long silent stretch, with no measurable change in cost.
check: Check that reminders follow the latest tool results, stay in the history to preserve cache and thinking blocks, and count silence across both text and progress updates.
quote: With `display: "updates"` set (the first lever), count consecutive tool-calling steps that give the user nothing to read: no `text` block and no progress-update text.

claim: For loosely specified Opus 5.5 workflows across connected apps, Anthropic suggests telling the model to explore relevant records with tools before acting.
why: In Anthropic’s multiapp automation tests, the instruction improved task completion at `medium` and `max` with slightly more tool calls and tokens.
check: Check whether loosely specified multiapp tasks include explore-first guidance and whether the records the agent searches contain untrusted content.
quote: Before taking any action, explore broadly with tool calls: list and open the emails, documents, spreadsheet tabs, and records across the available apps that could be relevant to this task

claim: For Opus 5.5 multiagent harnesses, give elapsed time against an estimated budget, or pair elapsed time alone with a prompt saying time matters when a budget is hard to estimate.
why: Both signals sped up small research teams versus an unsignaled single agent in Anthropic’s evaluations, and a tighter budget mostly kept more agents working in parallel.
check: Check whether a harness seeking faster turnaround reports elapsed time in its messages and tunes any budget against its own tasks.
quote: If you can estimate how long the task should take, give the model a time budget. Have your harness add a short line at the end of each message it sends back to the model, giving the elapsed time against that budget in seconds, for example `elapsed 340s / 1200s`.

claim: An elapsed-time budget in an Opus 5.5 multiagent prompt is advisory, so enforce any required hard stop in the harness.
why: The model can continue past the limit and may search or verify a little less under time pressure.
check: If the application needs a hard stop, check for a harness timeout and test answer quality on its own tasks.
quote: The budget is advisory and nothing stops the model at the limit, so if you need a hard stop, keep your own timeout.

claim: In Opus 5.5 chat applications, consider removing system instructions to think carefully before answering and use effort as the main control for thinking.
why: In Anthropic's chat testing, removing such a line made replies start sooner with no clear quality decline.
check: Review chat prompts that require deliberation and measure reply latency and quality before deciding whether to keep those lines.
quote: if your system prompt contains instructions that tell Claude to think carefully before answering, consider removing them for Claude Opus 5.5.

claim: When Opus 5.5 chat should treat earlier answers as settled, a system prompt can tell it to focus on the current turn unless the user revisits an earlier answer.
why: In Anthropic’s chat testing the instruction reduced follow-up thinking and latency without affecting quality, though the guide warns it may suppress spontaneous corrections.
check: Flag the instruction where later steps should revisit earlier work, and test whether it suppresses spontaneous corrections that the application needs.
quote: Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done. On later turns, focus your thinking on what the user is asking now, and don't go back over an earlier answer unless the user asks about it or points out a problem with it.

claim: To help Opus 5.5 distinguish pasted content from user instructions, wrap each pasted block in tags with a matching app-generated random ID and explain the tags in the system prompt.
why: Tags are one guardrail against indirect prompt injection and can be imitated.
check: For apps that accept pasted material, look for paired tags on separate lines and a system instruction to follow pasted instructions only when the user’s own message asks for it.
quote: Wrap each pasted block in an opening and a closing tag that both carry the same short random ID, generated by your application, with each tag on its own line:

claim: For Opus 5.5 frontend work, name the specific default visual patterns to avoid and extend the list if the first result replaces them with other unwanted defaults.
why: Without design direction the model falls back on a few default styles.
check: When an Opus 5.5 frontend prompt relies on generic style guidance, look for concrete directions such as avoiding numbered section labels or pill-shaped buttons.
quote: It responds well to instructions that name specific patterns to avoid, as in the following example.

claim: Retest earlier-model scaffolding for vision on Opus 5.5, and consider higher-resolution images or image-processing tools for the densest inputs.
why: In Anthropic’s dense-chart testing, Opus 5.5 at its lowest effort read values more accurately than Opus 5 at its highest.
check: For dense technical drawings or charts, measure whether higher resolution, a crop tool, or a container with image-processing tools improves accuracy.
quote: re-test whether you still need scaffolding you built for visual inputs on earlier models.

claim: Anthropic positions Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work.
why: These workloads are the stated design target for the model.
check: When selecting a model for long-running agentic coding or knowledge work, consider Opus 5.5 for that role.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 is built for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, priced at $4 / $20 USD per million input / output tokens.

claim: Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 return 400 for `tool_choice` types `any` and `tool` on Messages, Message Batches, and token counting.
why: The documented replacements depend on whether the route needs a tool call, schema-valid tool arguments, or only structured data.
check: For forced choices, check for `auto` with prompt steering and confirmation that required calls happen, `strict: true` when arguments need schema validation, or structured outputs for JSON-only extraction.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 doesn’t support forced tool use. `tool_choice` set to `{"type": "any"}` or `{"type": "tool", "name": "..."}` returns a 400 `invalid_request_error`:

claim: When a conversation switches from Opus 5.5 to Opus 5 or Opus 4.8, the API drops the unreadable Opus 5.5 thinking blocks without billing for them.
why: Compatibility depends on the model that produced the block and, for some compatible targets, the platform.
check: On model switches, keep passing blocks back unchanged and confirm that the target and platform support reading them if reasoning continuity is required.
quote: so a router switch, a client-side retry on another model, or a classifier-refusal fallback (server-side or SDK middleware) to Claude Opus 5 / Claude Opus 4.8 runs the turns after the switch without Claude Opus 5.5's reasoning.

claim: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable 5.1 enforce thinking-block prefix checks by default for accounts created on or after August 31, 2026, at 00:00 UTC.
why: On Messages, an enforced mismatch returns 400 by default, and `prefix_mismatch_behavior` can opt older accounts in or request dropped blocks where supported.
check: In custom `messages` builders, check for system prompt edits, deleted reminders, tool changes, or compaction that invalidates replayed blocks, and use append-only replacements where available.
quote: It is the history-editing check Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 run: enforced by default for accounts created on or after August 31, 2026, 00:00 UTC, and on older accounts only for requests that set `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior`.

claim: Opus 5.5 runs biology, cybersecurity, and reasoning-extraction classifiers, and a decline is reported with `stop_reason: refusal` and a category in `stop_details`.
why: The guide says Opus 5.5’s biology safeguards match Fable 5.1’s and are absent from Opus 5.
check: Check that refusal handling reads `stop_reason` and `stop_details`, and treats a `reasoning_extraction` decline as a response the server returns without retrying.
quote: A classifier decline arrives as a normal response with `stop_reason: "refusal"` and a `stop_details` object naming the category.

claim: Opus 5.5 rejects `computer_20251124` with a 400 on the Claude API, while Amazon Bedrock still accepts it with the `computer-use-2025-11-24` beta header.
why: The toolset replaces the older tool on the Claude API, and the linked migration guide documents the same replacement on Google Cloud.
check: When switching to `computer_toolset_20260801`, check the tool definition and handling of member calls, batch actions, and `toolset_name`.
quote: On Amazon Bedrock, Claude Opus 5.5 also accepts the `computer_20251124` tool with the `computer-use-2025-11-24` beta header. Claude Opus 5.5 returns a 400 error for any computer use tool version it doesn’t accept, such as `computer_20251124` on the Claude API.

claim: Opus 5.5 counts hidden thinking toward `max_tokens`, and the prompting guide reports that 128,000 worked well for long agentic coding turns in Anthropic’s testing.
why: A cap sized for Opus 5 with thinking off can cut replies short because hidden thinking uses part of the output budget.
check: For routes migrated from thinking off, check whether `max_tokens` leaves room for observed thinking and the full reply.
quote: a `max_tokens` of 128,000, the model’s maximum, has worked well in Anthropic’s testing

claim: The Opus 5.5 migration guide reports that a `max_tokens` cap of 64K has worked well for long agentic coding turns.
why: Thinking and reply tokens share the cap, and the prompting guide separately reports that 128,000 worked well in Anthropic’s testing.
check: Check whether the configured cap accommodates thinking plus the reply on representative long turns.
quote: For long agentic coding turns, 64K has worked well.

claim: When migrating to Opus 5.5, start with the existing Opus 5 verbosity, verification, and scope instructions, then retest each on your own evaluations.
why: The model behaviors those prompts compensated for may have changed.
check: Review whether legacy behavior-patching instructions were retested before deciding which to keep.
quote: may no longer be needed - keep them as the starting point, then re-test each on your own evals rather than carrying them over untouched.

claim: At `xhigh` and `max` Opus 5.5 turns run longer than on Opus 5, so timeouts, streaming and progress UX should be planned for that, and effort lowered before prompting for brevity.
why: Longer turns follow from the extra thinking at those levels.
check: Check timeouts and non-streaming calls in Opus 5.5 setups that use `xhigh` or `max`.
quote: turns run longer than on Claude Opus 5 - plan timeouts, streaming, and progress UX accordingly

claim: Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, below Opus 5's $5 and $25, with cache reads at $0.20 per million (0.05x input) and batch at half price.
why: The documented 0.05x cache-read rate makes cached input much cheaper than uncached input on Opus 5.5.
check: When comparing model costs for a setup, use these rates rather than Opus 5's, and check that cache-breaking edits are avoided.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 USD per million input tokens and $20 USD per million output tokens, below Claude Opus 5’s $5 and $25 USD

claim: Changing the top-level effort value between requests invalidates the cached messages on Opus 5.5; per-message effort (beta) changes it mid-conversation while keeping the cache.
why: Per-message effort is applied without editing the cached prefix.
check: If a harness switches effort between requests mid-session, flag the cache invalidation and suggest per-message effort.
quote: Changing the top-level `effort` value between requests invalidates the cached messages.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 defaults to `high` effort on the Claude API, but its effort levels represent different amounts of thinking than on Sonnet 5.
why: The guide recommends a fresh effort sweep because carrying over a level name can change thinking depth.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 setups migrated from Sonnet 5, check whether effort was re-evaluated rather than copied.
quote: Its levels are recalibrated: a level doesn’t produce the same amount of thinking as the same level on Claude Sonnet 5.

claim: For agentic coding and multistep tool use on Sonnet 5.5 start at `medium` for well-specified tasks and move to `high` for harder or longer ones; for chat and latency-sensitive work start at `medium` or `low`.
why: Higher effort means a longer wait before the reply starts.
check: Check whether Sonnet 5.5 effort was tuned to task difficulty and latency, and reserve `xhigh` or `max` for measured quality gains.
quote: For agentic coding and multistep tool use, start at `medium` for well-specified tasks and move to `high` for harder or longer ones.

claim: The Sonnet 5.5 migration guide suggests starting at `medium` for agentic coding and multistep tools and at `low` for chat, content generation, classification, extraction, and search.
why: The prompting guide suggests `medium` for well-specified agentic work, `low` or `medium` for latency-sensitive work, and `high` outside those categories.
check: Review whether the effort sweep included the suggested starting point for the workload.
quote: `medium` for agentic coding and multistep tool use; `low` for chat, content generation, classification, extraction, and search.

claim: At `medium` and above, Sonnet 5.5 thinks briefly before almost every reply and a system prompt to think less has almost no effect, while at `low` it skips thinking on most simple requests.
why: Thinking before a response delays the first visible token.
check: If a setup relies on a think-less prompt for latency at `medium` or above, check whether lower effort meets its latency and quality targets.
quote: From `medium` up, the model thinks briefly before almost every reply, even a greeting, which adds to the time before the first visible token, and a system-prompt request to think less has almost no effect at those levels.

claim: At `low` and `medium` effort on long agentic tasks Sonnet 5.5 is more likely to stop and check in with the user before finishing; at `low` it can also skip verifying a change.
why: Lower effort changes how it completes agentic work.
check: Check long agentic tasks at `low` or `medium` for premature check-ins and inspect code changes at `low` for missing verification.
quote: At `low` and `medium`, on long agentic tasks, it’s more likely to stop and check in with the user before it completes its work.

claim: If Sonnet 5.5 checks in early on agentic coding tasks at `low` or `medium`, try higher effort first or add a system instruction to carry work through at the current effort.
why: In the guide, the example prompt carries more work through at these efforts, resulting in longer and more expensive sessions.
check: If using the example, check that its stop-and-scope instructions sit alongside the existing rules for risky or irreversible actions.
quote: On agentic coding tasks at `low` and `medium` effort, the model sometimes checks in before the work is done. It might pause to confirm a plan, ask a question it could answer itself, or stop after one part of a multipart task to ask whether to continue. Try a higher effort level first. To keep the model working without changing effort, add this to your system prompt:

claim: Sonnet 5.5 tends to add unrequested tests, docs, or files at all effort levels, especially higher ones, and a scope-limiting system prompt reduces these additions at `xhigh` and `max`.
why: The requested change itself stays close to what was asked, but extras are added.
check: If a setup at `xhigh` or `max` requires minimal diffs, check for a prompt that tells the model to stop after checking the requested work.
quote: The model tends to add tests, documentation, and small supporting files that fit your repository’s conventions, even when you don’t ask for them.

claim: At `xhigh` and `max`, Sonnet 5.5 can start extra review rounds after finishing, so use `high` or below for routine work or prompt it to stop after the requested checks.
why: On coding tasks at `max`, Anthropic’s stop instruction prevented reviewer subagent launches and cut session cost by about a third with no quality change, though the main agent could still start reviews.
check: If extra review is unwanted at `xhigh` or `max`, check for a stop-and-report instruction or test lower effort.
quote: In testing on coding tasks at `max` effort, this stopped the model from launching reviewer subagents and cut session cost by about a third, with no change in quality.

claim: When an open-ended Sonnet 5.5 request should yield ideas or a plan, say so in the request or add a system instruction to wait for approval before building.
why: Without it the model can overreach on open-ended asks.
check: When a planning workflow produces artifacts prematurely, check whether either the user request or system prompt makes the expected stopping point explicit.
quote: When the user asks for ideas, options, or a plan, give them that and stop. Don't start building or changing anything until they say to go ahead.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 rejects `thinking.type: disabled` with a 400 and supports `between_tools` to turn off up-front thinking at `high` effort or below.
why: Sonnet 5.5 replaced `disabled` with `between_tools`, which keeps short progress updates but does no up-front thinking.
check: Check for `disabled` requests or `between_tools` combined with `xhigh`, `max`, extra `thinking` fields, or a per-message effort value that differs from the active level.
quote: To run Claude Sonnet 5.5 without up-front thinking, send `thinking: {"type": "between_tools"}`. It’s the lowest thinking setting on this model, and it’s accepted at `high` effort or below.

claim: `between_tools` thinking is accepted only by Sonnet 5.5, so a router or retry that re-sends the same request body to another model must drop the field first.
why: Other models reject it with a 400.
check: In multi-model routers or subagent fallbacks that reuse request bodies, check that `between_tools` is stripped for non-Sonnet-5.5 targets.
quote: client-side code that re-sends the same body to another model (a router or a retry) must drop the field first.

claim: For a Sonnet 5 route that disabled thinking, try Sonnet 5.5 with adaptive thinking at `low` first, and use `between_tools` at `high` or below if the route must stay without up-front thinking.
why: At `low` with adaptive thinking, Sonnet 5.5 keeps thinking short and skips it on most simple requests.
check: Check latency and quality when trialing adaptive `low`, and remove no-thinking instructions when using `between_tools` because they make visible internal XML tags more likely.
quote: Remove any instruction that tells the model not to think - such instructions make it more likely to write internal XML tags in its visible output.

claim: For JSON tasks that require several reasoning steps, Sonnet 5.5 often skips thinking, especially at `low` or `medium`, and adaptive thinking with a think-first prompt can raise accuracy.
why: Structured outputs reserve response text for JSON, and the guide reports the highest accuracy for these tasks at adaptive `xhigh` with higher output-token use than `high`.
check: On these JSON routes, measure accuracy with the prompt or at adaptive `xhigh` and treat `stop_reason: max_tokens` as a failure even when the text is valid JSON.
quote: On tasks like these, the model often answers without thinking first, particularly at `low` and `medium` effort.

claim: On chat and knowledge-work tasks, Sonnet 5.5 sometimes answers from training knowledge when a web search would catch changed details.
why: Details such as what is allowed, required or charged may have changed since training.
check: For research or support agents on Sonnet 5.5 with search tools, check for an instruction to verify changeable specifics.
quote: On chat and knowledge-work tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 sometimes answers from its training knowledge when a web search would catch details that have changed.

claim: For Sonnet 5.5 chat and knowledge work, remove prompt language discouraging tool use and, if search is available, ask the model to verify changeable details.
why: The guide observes that the model sometimes answers from training when a search would catch changed details.
check: Review tool-minimizing wording and search guidance on research or support routes that rely on current details.
quote: First, check your prompt for language that discourages tool use, such as “only use tools when strictly necessary” or “minimize tool calls,” and remove it.

claim: After recalibrating effort on Sonnet 5.5, try removing Sonnet 5 workarounds for refusals, tool calls, or low initiative and rerun evaluations before further prompt tuning.
why: The model is stronger at multistep agentic coding, uses connected tools more reliably, declines fewer benign requests and holds a system-prompt role better.
check: When reviewing inherited workarounds, look for a Sonnet 5.5 evaluation with the relevant wording or shim removed.
quote: The model is strongest on multistep agentic coding in a real repository, uses connected tools more reliably in agentic workflows, declines fewer benign requests, and holds a system-prompt role more reliably when a user pastes in a competing persona.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 may misread mid-turn user input as injection if it is inside a `tool_result` or delivered as a system message immediately after one.
why: The model is trained to resist indirect prompt injection and pays attention to where text sits relative to tool results.
check: Check that mid-turn input appears as text after the last `tool_result` in the user message and that any harness notice follows in a separate system message.
quote: Sometimes it treats a genuine user message as a possible injection. Suppose a message the user typed mid-task reaches the model as a [mid-conversation system message](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages) placed directly after a tool result, or inside a `tool_result` block.

claim: The Sonnet 5.5 prompting guide reports no observed injection misread from built-in task budgets, while the migration guide says their countdown can cause one.
why: Both guides warn about custom countdowns after tool results in interactive sessions, but they give different advice on built-in budgets.
check: Flag custom per-tool countdowns in interactive sessions and, following the prompting guide, try removing a built-in task budget if the misread occurs.
quote: In interactive sessions where users can type mid-turn, don’t add your own token or budget countdown after tool results. [Task budgets](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets) (in beta) add a similar countdown, but they haven’t been seen to cause this misread. If you see the misread while a task budget is set, try the session without one.

claim: The Sonnet 5.5 migration guide warns that built-in task budgets and harness text appended after every tool result can make the model suspect prompt injection.
why: The migration guide attributes the risk to per-step placement, while the prompting guide has not observed this misread with the built-in countdown.
check: Following the migration guidance, check for per-step text and task budgets in interactive sessions where users can type mid-turn.
quote: Task budgets can cause this, because the budget countdown arrives as a system message after every tool result

claim: If Sonnet 5.5 reports code changes complete without test or build output, add a system instruction requiring a check that exercises the change before reporting it done.
why: At `low`, the guide reports that the example instruction made skipped or superficial checks rare at slightly higher cost per task, with no measurable quality change.
check: Review completion reports lacking test or build output, and check that the prompt calls for a project test, type check, build, or execution of the changed command.
quote: If you see changes reported as complete without test or build output in the transcript, add this paragraph, or one like it, to the system prompt.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 sometimes changes the case of a tool name or slightly changes a parameter name, so accept unambiguous matches or return an `is_error: true` tool result with the expected name.
why: The model usually corrects the call on its next turn.
check: Check that the dispatcher either accepts an unambiguous name match or returns an actionable tool error with the exact expected name.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 occasionally calls a declared tool by a name that differs only in letter case, such as `bash` for `Bash`.

claim: Crop, zoom, or image-code tools help Sonnet 5.5 read dense charts at every effort level and technical drawings at `high` or above.
why: In Anthropic’s chart testing, tools at `high` gave better accuracy than `max` without tools at a fraction of the cost.
check: Check for image-processing options on dense visual tasks and test both tooling and effort on technical drawings.
quote: On charts, the tools help at every effort level. On technical drawings, they help only from `high` effort up, and most at `xhigh` and `max`.

claim: When server-side fallback is enabled in beta, Sonnet 5.5 retries `cyber` and `frontier_llm` declines on Sonnet 5 and skips retries for `bio`, `reasoning_extraction`, and `general_harms`.
why: Refusal responses carry `stop_reason: refusal` and a `stop_details.category` identifying the policy area.
check: Check that Sonnet 5.5 code branches on `stop_reason` and handles non-retried categories.
quote: (in beta), it retries `cyber` and `frontier_llm` declines on Claude Sonnet 5. It doesn’t retry `bio`, `reasoning_extraction`, or `general_harms` declines.

claim: For the hardest long-horizon work, the Sonnet 5.5 migration guide recommends an Opus model.
why: The recommendation applies to the workload’s difficulty and horizon.
check: Review whether the setup has considered an Opus model for its hardest long-horizon tasks.
quote: for the hardest long-horizon work, an Opus model is the better choice.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 returns 400 for `tool_choice` types `any` and `tool`, including on the token-counting endpoint.
why: `auto` and `none` remain supported.
check: Check outgoing Sonnet 5.5 requests for forced `tool_choice`, including token-counting requests.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 doesn’t support forced tool use. `tool_choice` set to `{"type": "any"}` or `{"type": "tool", "name": "..."}` returns a 400 `invalid_request_error`:

claim: A Sonnet 5.5 advisor-tool executor returns 400 with advisors Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5, or Haiku 5.5.
why: Both pages give the same allowed list, while the migration guide explicitly lists Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 among rejections and the what’s-new page explicitly lists Haiku 5.5.
check: For advisor-tool setups with a Sonnet 5.5 executor, check the advisor model is an accepted one.
quote: Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Haiku 5.5 advisors work with a Claude Sonnet 5 executor. With a Claude Sonnet 5.5 executor, they return a 400 `invalid_request_error`.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 supports mid-conversation system messages, mid-conversation tool changes in beta, and per-message effort in beta, all unavailable on Sonnet 5.
why: The features give harnesses ways to append instruction, tool, and effort changes during a session.
check: Check whether Sonnet 5.5 harnesses that need mid-session changes use these features before rewriting earlier messages.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5 doesn’t support per-message effort, mid-conversation system messages, or mid-conversation tool changes.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5’s prices except for cache reads, which cost $0.10 per million tokens, half the Sonnet 5 rate.
why: The migration guide separately reports that Sonnet 5.5 at `medium` outscored Sonnet 5 at `high` in most agentic coding evaluations, typically at under a fifth of the cost.
check: When estimating Sonnet 5.5 cost, use cost per completed task at the chosen effort level.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 has the same prices as Claude Sonnet 5, except for prompt cache reads, which cost $0.10 USD per million tokens, half the Claude Sonnet 5 rate.

claim: For Sonnet 5.5 multi-turn chat that should treat previous answers as settled, add a system instruction to focus on the current question unless the user revisits an earlier answer.
why: The model otherwise may re-examine earlier answers on each new turn.
check: Check whether the instruction is absent where the model must revisit earlier work, such as analyses or agentic tasks whose later steps can reveal earlier errors.
quote: Once Claude has answered something, Claude treats that answer as done. On later turns Claude's thinking goes to what the person is asking now, and Claude doesn't go back over an earlier answer unless the person asks about it or points out a problem with it.

claim: Anthropic positions Haiku 5.5 for high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, routing, extraction, and subagent tasks.
why: These tasks exemplify the model’s priority on volume and response time.
check: When selecting a model for a high-volume, latency-sensitive role, consider Haiku 5.5 and measure it on the workload.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, routing, extraction, and subagent tasks.

claim: Haiku 5.5 defaults to `medium` effort and rejects requests with the manual `budget_tokens` setting from Haiku 4.5 with a 400.
why: There is no old setting to carry over; sweep two or three levels on your own evals.
check: Check migration code for `budget_tokens` and compare two or three effort levels on representative tasks.
quote: On Claude Haiku 5.5, a request that sets `budget_tokens` returns a 400 error.

claim: On Haiku 5.5, start most work at `medium` and reserve `xhigh` or `max` for workloads with measured gains worth the higher cost.
why: Thinking and replies get much longer at `xhigh` and `max`, so Anthropic recommends comparing those settings against Sonnet 5.5.
check: Test `low` for chat, short tool tasks, or simple high-volume requests, `medium` for most work including agentic coding, and `high` for knowledge work, longer tasks, or strict instruction following.
quote: `xhigh` and `max` are for work where a quality gain on your evals justifies the cost. Thinking and replies get much longer at these levels, so also run your evals on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and compare performance, cost, and speed.

claim: Haiku 5.5 has thinking on by default and counts thinking toward `max_tokens`, so a cap sized for Haiku 4.5 with thinking off can cut replies short.
why: Hidden thinking uses part of the same limit as the visible reply.
check: For migrated routes, test whether `max_tokens` leaves room for the expected thinking and reply.
quote: Thinking is on by default and counts toward `max_tokens`, which can go up to 128,000. A `max_tokens` value sized for Claude Haiku 4.5 requests that ran without thinking can cut the reply off, so leave room for thinking.

claim: Anthropic recommends lowering effort to reduce thinking on Haiku 5.5 after an answer-directly prompt failed to stop thinking in testing.
why: Shorter thinking at lower effort is the documented way to trade response quality for latency or cost.
check: If a route relies on an answer-directly prompt to limit thinking, measure lower effort on the same workload.
quote: In Anthropic’s testing, telling the model in the prompt to answer directly didn’t stop it from thinking.

claim: Haiku 5.5 accepts `thinking.type: disabled` at `low`, `medium`, and `high`, and returns 400 for it at `xhigh` or `max`.
why: Per-message changes in effort need adaptive thinking, so a change to a different level with thinking disabled also returns 400.
check: Check disabled-thinking routes for `xhigh`, `max`, or a per-message effort change from the level already in effect.
quote: This works at `low`, `medium`, and `high` only. At `xhigh` and `max`, the request returns a 400 error.

claim: At `xhigh` in multi-turn chat, Haiku 5.5 sometimes writes the whole answer in its thinking and ends the turn without visible text.
why: Checking for visible text catches empty replies even when the model has generated thinking.
check: If this behavior appears in multi-turn chat at `xhigh`, check responses for an empty visible reply.
quote: At `xhigh` effort in multi-turn chats, the model sometimes writes its whole answer in its thinking and ends the turn with no visible text.

claim: When Haiku 5.5 has a search tool, give it today's date in the system prompt or the tool description, rendered once at conversation start.
why: In Anthropic's testing this grounded answers in recent search results.
check: Check for a date in the initial system prompt or tool description and, if the session crosses into another day, supply the new date in the newest turn.
quote: When you give Claude Haiku 5.5 a search tool, also give it today’s date.

claim: Haiku 5.5 sometimes needs a targeted search nudge after the date, especially at `low` effort and with long system prompts, and the guide says a short prompt can omit it.
why: In Anthropic’s testing, the nudge increased searches on questions with changed answers and added searches in only 0–3 percent of tries on prompts that needed none.
check: If the model skips searches for changeable facts, test a targeted cue and check whether the date alone suffices with a short system prompt.
quote: The model also sometimes needs an extra nudge to search. This occurs most at `low` effort and with long system prompts. To fix it, add this text directly after the date:

claim: With thinking disabled, Haiku 5.5 can skip a needed tool call when the same request also uses structured outputs for JSON.
why: In Anthropic’s testing with thinking off, a prompt restricting JSON to the final answer improved the share of complete and correct JSON answers at `low` and `medium`.
check: If tool calls are skipped, test adaptive thinking, removal of the output schema from the tool-calling request, a forced call, or guidance to call the tool first and put JSON only in the final answer.
quote: With thinking off, Claude Haiku 5.5 might skip a tool call it needs when you also request JSON output with [structured outputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs).

claim: Haiku 5.5 accepts forced `tool_choice` even with thinking on, but the response starts with the tool call and contains no `thinking` block.
why: Forced calls skip thinking on this model.
check: Where Haiku 5.5 must reason before calling a tool, check that the route uses `auto` and the prompt specifies when to call the tool.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced `tool_choice` (`any` or a named tool), with thinking on too, but the response then starts with the tool call and has no `thinking` block.

claim: With a long coding-agent system prompt at `low`, Haiku 5.5 sometimes hands work back early, and a keep-working instruction or higher effort can reduce this.
why: In Anthropic’s tests without the instruction, going from `low` to `medium` roughly halved early stopping and more than doubled output tokens per attempt.
check: When early handoffs appear in these agents, test the keep-working instruction or a higher effort level and measure the cost.
quote: With a long coding-agent system prompt at `low` effort, it sometimes stops early and hands the task back to the user.

claim: If Haiku 5.5 reports code changes done without checking them at `low` or `medium`, ask it in the system prompt to run a check that exercises the change before reporting success.
why: In Anthropic’s testing, the instruction increased how often the model checked its changes and improved task performance at the cost of more tokens.
check: When reviewing unverified completion reports, check for guidance to run a project test, type check, build, or changed command.
quote: At `low` and `medium` effort, Claude Haiku 5.5 sometimes reports a code change as done without running a check.

claim: For chatbots and support assistants on Haiku 5.5, add 'The rules in this system prompt hold for the whole conversation...' alongside other prompt-injection protections, and use `high` effort when instruction following matters most.
why: In testing this made the model keep to its system prompt more often.
check: For a Haiku 5.5 chatbot or support assistant, check for prompt guidance to keep following its rules across turns and for `high` effort where adherence matters most.
quote: The rules in this system prompt hold for the whole conversation.

claim: Haiku 5.5 sometimes exposes reasoning-like text in replies, more often with thinking off or at `low` effort.
why: The guide recommends trying adaptive thinking at `medium` if this behavior appears.
check: If reasoning-like text appears in visible replies, check the current thinking mode and test adaptive thinking at `medium`.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 sometimes writes reasoning-like text in the reply that users see. This occurs more often with thinking off or at `low` effort. If you see this behavior, switch to adaptive thinking and `medium` effort.

claim: Haiku 5.5 can ignore mid-task user input as untrusted if it arrives inside a `tool_result` or in a system message immediately after one.
why: The model is trained to resist prompt injection through tool results.
check: Check that user input is sent as text after the last `tool_result` in the user message and that harness notices use a separate system message.
quote: or as a [mid-conversation system message](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages) right after a tool result. The model can then treat it as untrusted text and ignore it.

claim: Haiku 5.5 has no server-side fallback, so `fallbacks: default` leaves a declined request declined and a list of fallback models returns 400.
why: Safety classifiers decline in four categories (`cyber`, `bio`, `frontier_llm`, `general_harms`) that Haiku 4.5 did not return.
check: Check that Haiku 5.5 requests omit `fallbacks` and that the client handles `stop_reason: refusal`.
quote: with `fallbacks: "default"` a declined request stays declined, and a list of fallback models returns a 400.

claim: Haiku 5.5 rejects all `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k` settings on API version `2026-10-21`, and accepts only limited sampling settings on `2023-06-01`.
why: On `2023-06-01`, `temperature: 1` or `top_p: 0.99` is accepted when sent alone, and `top_k` is always rejected.
check: Check outgoing sampling parameters against their API version and use structured outputs or an enum-valued tool to replace `temperature: 0` on classification routes.
quote: `temperature` must be `1`, and `top_p` must be `0.99`, its default; any other value of either returns a 400 (a `top_p` of `1` included), and so does any `top_k` value, and so does a request that sends both `temperature` and `top_p`. This holds on every request, whether or not thinking is used. On API version `2026-10-21`, any value of any of the three returns a 400.

claim: Haiku 5.5 returns 400 for assistant prefill even with thinking off, so end `messages` with a user turn.
why: Prefill is no longer supported.
check: Replace trailing assistant turns with structured outputs or enum tools for format, system guidance for preambles, or user-turn continuations and reminders, as appropriate.
quote: A prefill is a final assistant turn in `messages` that the model continues. Claude Haiku 4.5 accepts one when thinking is off. Claude Haiku 5.5 rejects it with a 400, with thinking turned off too. End `messages` with a user turn, and replace each prefill according to what it was for:

claim: Haiku 5.5’s newer tokenizer yields approximately 30% more tokens for the same input than Haiku 4.5, with the exact increase depending on the text.
why: An old `max_tokens` cap may cut off equivalent output, and cost depends on the resulting token count and its rate card.
check: Check cost estimates and context budgets moved to Haiku 5.5 were recounted with `count_tokens` on the new model.
quote: the same input text produces approximately 30% more tokens, and the exact increase depends on the content.

claim: Haiku 5.5 has two price tiers by prompt length: $0.10 / $0.50 per million input/output tokens for prompts of 100K tokens or fewer and $0.50 / $2.50 above that, versus a flat $1 / $5 on Haiku 4.5.
why: The higher rate applies once the prompt exceeds 100K tokens.
check: Check that Haiku 5.5 cost estimates use the rate card for the prompt’s length.
quote: $0.10 / $0.50 per MTok input / output when the prompt is 100K tokens or fewer, and $0.50 / $2.50 when it is longer

claim: By default, Haiku 5.5 retains earlier assistant turns’ thinking blocks in context as input tokens, while Haiku 4.5 kept only the latest turn’s blocks.
why: Retained thinking can add input tokens on multi-turn conversations beyond the tokenizer change itself.
check: If retained thinking is driving input growth, consider thinking block clearing.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 keeps thinking blocks from all earlier assistant turns in context, and they count as input tokens.

claim: Add Haiku 5.5’s new system-prompt instructions at the start of a conversation, since changing the prompt when replaying earlier thinking blocks can return 400.
why: A resumed session can receive new instructions in its newest turn or through an appended system message on supported platforms.
check: Check that a resumed conversation replaying thinking blocks receives new instructions without rewriting its original system prompt.
quote: Add it to new conversations only. If you resume a stored conversation with a new system prompt and send its thinking blocks back, the request can return a 400 error.

claim: The migration guide keeps Opus 5.5 as the default model for new code and says to target Haiku 5.5 when the user asks for Haiku or for a fast, low-cost model.
why: It sets a model-selection default for new work.
check: For new code that selects a Claude model, check the default when the user names no model and check for Haiku 5.5 when they request Haiku or a fast, low-cost model.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 stays the default model for new code; target Claude Haiku 5.5 when the user asks for Haiku or for a fast, low-cost model.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 rejects `computer_20251124` on the Claude API in favor of `computer_toolset_20260801`, while Amazon Bedrock still accepts the older tool with its beta header.
why: The linked migration guide documents the same toolset requirement on Google Cloud, and changing to the toolset requires changes to the agent loop.
check: Check computer-use definitions by platform and verify migrated loops handle member calls, batch actions, and `toolset_name`.
quote: On Amazon Bedrock, Claude Sonnet 5.5 also accepts the `computer_20251124` tool with the `computer-use-2025-11-24` beta header. Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns a 400 error for any computer use tool version it doesn’t accept, such as `computer_20251124` on the Claude API.

claim: With a Sonnet 5.5 advisor-tool executor, accepted advisors return encrypted advice as `advisor_redacted_result` blocks.
why: The client cannot read the advice text in these blocks.
check: Check that the client handles `advisor_redacted_result` without expecting plaintext advice.
quote: Every advisor that Claude Sonnet 5.5 accepts returns its advice encrypted, as an `advisor_redacted_result` block. So your client can’t read the advice text.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 has a minimum cacheable prompt size of 512 tokens, down from 1,024 on Sonnet 5.
why: Prompts between those minimums can qualify for caching after migration to Sonnet 5.5.
check: Use the model-specific minimum when assessing whether a short prompt is eligible for caching.
quote: with a minimum cacheable prompt of 512 tokens

claim: Avoid blanket instructions to search for all present-day factual questions on Haiku 5.5.
why: In Anthropic’s testing, a blanket rule caused searches on half of the prompts that needed none without improving correctness.
check: Look for blanket search instructions and check whether they trigger tool calls on requests that do not need search.
quote: that instruction made the model search on half of the prompts that needed no search. It didn’t produce more correct answers.
